Constructs: 52 items about affect (in footnote 1, also referred to as sub-threshold symptoms of psychopathology): 17 positive (I slept well, I was physically active, I am looking forward to tomorrow, I felt like others liked me, I was social, My concentration was good, I felt at ease with others, I felt appreciated, I felt relaxed, Everything came easy, I felt like undertaking things, I could handle the things that confronted me, I felt energetic, I could enjoy things, I was happy, My day was worth living, I felt good) and 35 negative (I experienced physical pain, I was impulsive, I experienced physical discomfort, I was unable to sit still, I was bored quickly, I felt tired, I’m dreading something that will happen soon, Things did not bother me, I had a fight, I was easily startled, I felt impatient, I could not bring myself to do anything, I avoided things, I had difficulty making decisions, I felt rebellious, Others felt annoyed by me, I was afraid of making mistakes, I felt suspicious, I felt nervous, I felt guilty, I felt lonely, I felt irritated, It bothered me that things did not go as expected, I felt empty, I felt overstimulated, I felt strange, I was easily distracted, I felt overburdened, I had moodswings, I worried, My thoughts would not leave me alone, I felt restless, I was easily upset, I felt stressed, I felt down)

StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
The authors examined AR patterns for each of the 52 items assessed. They used two methods: time-varying AR (via generalized additive models) and moving window. They conceptualized an EWS as a significant rise in AR 1 or 2 weeks before a sudden transition in mental health (identified via change-point analyses). 

For the GAM: gradual changes in parameters were estimated using non-parametric smooth functions based on thin-plate regression splines, and sudden transitions were modeled by adding a dummy predictor for time of transition. To check whether change in AR was significantly increasing or decreasing, the authors computed the first derivative of the smooth function and examined whether a confidence interval around it included zero (pg. 1029-1030). They examined 4 types of GAM models: with more conservative (.95% CI) or liberal (.90 CI) thresholds for including zero, and the proximity of EWS (1 vs 2 weeks). 

For moving windows, they detrended data and then determined whether there was a rise in AR based on Kendall's τ. They varied: the window size (14 vs 21 vs 28) and the number of estimates to compute Kendall's τ (14 vs 21).
GeneralNotes:
For preregistration: Wrote 'timing unclear' because say they already collected data' but don't specify is this was before or after data access. 

Regarding comparisons between models: They do not choose a final model but instead compare results to see if the two methods perform similarly in identifying rising AR before sudden drops in mental health (the two models do not). As such not including this as model comparison.

StudyTopic: Mental health,Emotions,Physical health and health behaviour

(2 patients completed 3 months of ESM as they were part of a pilot, and the rest completed on average 18 weeks or 4.5 months of ESM)
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:

Main analysis: Moving window, window size of 2 weeks (i.e., 70 observations). "Autoregressive coefficient calculated at lag-1 over the residuals obtained after detrending (Dakos et al., 2012)." Did not compute lagged association between evening observation and next morning observation. 

Significance testing on whether AR increased: Kendall correlation coefficient in the two weeks prior to the transition. Calculated positive and negative predictive values following Altman & Bland to estimate sensitivity and specificity. Also estimated false positives in individuals without a transition in symptoms.

Authors: Alessandri, G., De Longis, E., & Doane, L. D.
Title: Associations between inertia of negative emotions and diurnal cortisol in a sample of college students
Reference: Alessandri, G., De Longis, E., & Doane, L. D. (2021). Associations between inertia of negative emotions and diurnal cortisol in a sample of college students. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 134, 105427. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psyneuen.2021.105427
Definition_ExactPhrase:
Abstract: “High emotional inertia, characterized by emotional states that carry over from one moment to the next” (page 1)

Introduction: “tendency of emotional states to be self-predictable over time and to be resistant to change, a condition called emotional inertia (Kuppens et al., 2010, Suls et al., 1998). Low levels of emotional inertia indicate higher tendency to change, while high levels indicate emotional states that persist from one moment to the next (Kuppens et al., 2010). Emotional inertia is usually measured by using the autocorrelation, or the autoregressive effect, of an emotion across time, which indicates the degree to which a current emotional state can be predicted by a previous emotional state and it is almost insensitive to the emotional level (Wang et al., 2012). Higher autocorrelations indicate more inert and self-predictive emotions, suggesting that any possible deviation from the mean is likely to persist for a long period of time. Conversely, low autocorrelations suggest low interdependency of repeated measures of an emotion, indicating that emotional states are relatively unpredictable over time (Wang et al., 2012).” (page 2)

In methods: "in accordance with our perspective, the estimated within-individual autoregressive coefficient represented a direct conceptualization of inertia as a trait-level, between-individual difference." (page 3)

OperationalizeRecovery_How: Statistically (e.g., discuss speed of return or specific statistical terms such as mean)

Authors: Mey, L. K., Wenzel, M., Morello, K., Rowland, Z., Kubiak, T., & Tüscher, O.
Title: Be Kind to Yourself: The Implications of Momentary Self-Compassion for Affective Dynamics and Well-Being in Daily Life
Reference: Mey, L. K., Wenzel, M., Morello, K., Rowland, Z., Kubiak, T., & Tüscher, O. (2023). Be Kind to Yourself: The Implications of Momentary Self-Compassion for Affective Dynamics and Well-Being in Daily Life. Mindfulness, 14(3), 622–636. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12671-022-02050-y
Definition_ExactPhrase: “Lingering in these past affective states may indicate a “resistance to emotional change” (Kuppens et al., 2010, p. 985), also called emotional inertia, which is the extent to which affective states are carried over from one moment to the next (e.g., Koval & Kuppens, 2012). High emotional inertia of both PA and NA demonstrates an impaired ability to flexibly regulate one’s emotions in response to changing situational requirements, thus depriving emotions from its adaptive purpose (Koval et al., 2015, Kuppens et al., 2010). Accordingly, high emotional inertia is connected to mental disorders such as depression (Kuppens et al., 2010) as well as to lower overall well-being, with NA inertia showing stronger and more consistent results than PA inertia (Houben et al., 2015, Koval et al., 2015).” (pg. 624)
Definition_ComponentsUnique_other: Inflexibity,impaired emotion regulation,connected to mental disorders
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase: 7 days of ESM prompts (other waves not included in this study), with six semi-random signals. These were sent in a 12-hour timeframe each day, starting at 8, 9, or 10 AM (depending on the participant's preference), with signals at least 60 minutes apart but otherwise randomly generated. (pg. 625 & 626)
WithinPersonChange_Correlate: Internal context (e.g., thoughts, rumination, deep breathing)
WithinPersonChange_Moderator_ExactInfo: The moderator was self-compassion, measured via a scale they designed (as there was no validated measure when they began the study). They used six items, with each representing one of the six subscales of the trait self-compassion: self-kindness, self-judgment, common humanity, isolation, mindfulness, over-identification (all on a scale from 0-100), and reversed relevant items then averaged all items to a total score (pg. 626). They examined how this variable interacted with NA/PA inertia with one model, and also examined in another model the interaction of PA/NA inertia with both positive and negative self-compassion (dividing the items into two subscales).
WithinPersonChange_StatisticalModel: AR model with time-varying interaction term
StatisticalModelFamily: AR model with other main parameter (e.g. ARX)
CenterPredictors_How: They within-person standardize predictors & outcomes: "instead of implementing within-person centering, we within-person standardized all level-1 predictors and outcomes by taking the difference between the score of an observation and the person mean of this variable and dividing it by the person standard deviation of this variable. This approach facilitates the interpretation of the effect sizes and better controls for between-person differences in the estimates of the slopes compared to within-person centering (Wang et al., 2019)" (pg. 628)
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
Authors estimated “two-level models with random intercepts and slopes” and when possible had an unstructured covariance matrix "to allow for random covariation between random intercepts and slopes (Robson & Pevalin, 2016)" (pg. 627). They replaced the first signal of each day with a missing value for the lagged values. They included the EMA signal number (across the study) "as a fixed effect to control for possible time trends" and controlled for other variables (daily hassle strain). 

They carried out separate models for PA and NA, and one with SC as a total score and another with both SC-Neg and SC-pos. They assessed within-person change by including an interaction term between PA/NA inertia and SC.

Note for whether results provide evidence for within-person change in inertia: no, but that's just whether it changes alongside self-compassion, as it's not assessed any other way...

Note for definition: The authors specifically mention AR in relation to inertia in the methods section, but specifically as an operationalization (not as a definition), so not including it in the definition components.

Authors: Schreuder, M. J., Ariens, S., Lafit, G., & Ceulemans, E.

Reference: Schreuder, M. J., Ariens, S., Lafit, G., & Ceulemans, E. (2025). Bouncing back from emotional ups and downs: Insights in emotional recovery using survival analyses of burst ESM data. Cognition and Emotion, 39(4), 910–919. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699931.2024.2423706
Definition_ExactPhrase:
Intro: 
“After such events, both positive and negative emotions may return to their respective baselines (i.e. mean levels), which is termed emotional recovery.” (page 910)
OperationalizeRecovery_How: Conceptually,Statistically (e.g., discuss speed of return or specific statistical terms such as mean)
OperationalizeRecovery_How_ExactPhrase:
“After such events, both positive and negative emotions may return to their respective baselines (i.e. mean levels), which is termed emotional recovery.” (page 910)
And in general, the paper as a whole examines how to define the thresholds participants return to (e.g., baseline from current two weeks, or prior two weeks)
In addition, run sensitivity analyses "in which we defined people’s emotional baseline as the mode and median (instead of the mean)." (page 913)
SamplingDesign_Type_other: Burst design based on threshold from prior answers
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase: Over three weeks, 8 fixed prompts a day at equidistant time intervals (further timing info not specified). From the second week on, in addition to these 8 fixed prompts, "participants could receive bursts that were triggered whenever participants reported a score below their own lower limit (i.e. feeling very bad) or a score above their own upper limit (i.e. feeling very good), these limits were calculated based on participants' first week of responses" (15th percentile for lower limit, 85th for upper). Bursts "consisted of four beeps delivered at 10-minute intervals” (page 912)
WithinPersonChange_Correlate: Internal context (e.g., thoughts, rumination, deep breathing), External context (e.g., specific events), Appraisal (e.g., rating of how un/pleasant an event was)
WithinPersonChange_Moderator_ExactInfo:
Resilience on that day (answered in final beep of each day), via 8 questions all rated on a scale from 0-100. Items derived from Connor Davidson Resilience Scale (CDRS) (Connor & Davidson, 2003), a trait resilience scale, but “slightly rephrased in order to cover the past day” (page 912)
Exact items are on OSF: https://osf.io/afhkp/files/pmynr.

Other variables directly predicting return times: 
Type of episode (valence)
In second model (but still with these predictors in the same model as estimating return times, so in "one" modeling step):
occurrence of earlier negative or positive episodes, episode intensity, occurrence of cumulative episodes
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
Survival analysis. Multilevel Cox proportional hazard models. Participants' thresholds were computed based on mean levels from final two weeks of ESM data (i.e., when bursts occurred, rather than first week of ESM data, which determined thresholds for bursts in ESM data collection). Returns to baseline were defined as "the earliest moment at which participants reported a score above baseline (negative episode) or below baseline (positive episode, Supplement Fig. S2). In case returns did not occur before the next missing observation or before the end of the day, they were considered right censored." (page 912). Missing observations within bursts were carried forward (i.e., copied) to limit the number of right-censored events, leading to imputations in 13% of all emotion ratings. Return times in model were predicted by: trait resilience, day resilience, type of episode (pos vs neg), interaction between trait resilience & episode type, and interaction between daily resilience & episode type. Random intercepts included. 

Second step: Included 4 additional predictors: earlier pos/neg episodes, episode intensity, and occurrence of cumulative episodes. 

Sensitivity analyses: rerun all analyses without imputed/carried-forward data. Baseline defined as mean or median (instead of mean)

Model building: "Compared a model with random intercepts vs an empty model (without random effects) or a more complex model (with random slopes for daily resilience, which was the analysis that was preregistration). These models were compared with likelihood ratio tests and the best fitting model was that with just random intercepts, so that was the main model the authors used for analyses (but the model with random slopes is reported in Table S3 in supplementary materials)." Info found on page 917, footnote 4

For moderators (within-person predictors) of AR parameters, we indicated that these are all done in one step, as although the authors examine these in two separate models, they indicate that they are estimating return times in the same model as these predictors. Second, we write that these are all indicated by participants, as even though variables relating to episodes (such as 'occurrence of earlier negative or positive episodes') are determined via a threshold the researchers define, the actual data these thresholds are based on are from participants' ESM responses.

Title: Combining experience sampling with temporal network analysis to understand inertia of negative emotion in dysphoria.
Reference: Chen, T., Wang, P., Wang, Y., & Irish, M. (2023). Combining experience sampling with temporal network analysis to understand inertia of negative emotion in dysphoria. Journal of Affective Disorders, 338, 246–253. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2023.06.006
Definition_ExactPhrase: "The resistance to change of emotional state over time, or emotional inertia (Kuppens et al., 2010, Suls et al., 1998), is conceptualised as one such maladaptive expression of emotional dynamics (Kuppens et al., 2010)." (pg 246)
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase: 10 beeps delivered semi-randomly from 10AM to 10PM each day, for 7 consecutive days (pg. 248)
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
As their main analysis, the authors computed a multilevel VAR model as a temporal network analysis. In addition to the three discrete emotion variables, they also included 6 emotion regulation variables. They compared whether inertia was different between the two groups (control & dysphoric) via independent t-tests. 

The authors used listwise deletion for missing data. They applied linear detrending for each ESM variable that did not meet the assumption of stationarity. For the mlVAR model, they used the orthogonal estimation approach for temporal network estimation since +6 variables were selected in the study. Since the mlVAR package doesn't allow adding subject-level covariates, they estimated a separate multilevel VAR (via mle4) to control for sex and the average individual-level negative emotion intensity. (However, when looking at results for this in Table S2, it looks like this was maybe with a model where the discrete emotions predicted other discrete emotions?)
GeneralNotes:
The authors include information about AR in relation to inertia, but specifically frame it as an operationalization, so not including it in the definition. 

In the discussion, the authors also note that via the operationalization of inertia as AR, they're unable to fully understand inertia and "whether the resistance to change is voluntary or unvoluntary" 

Full quote: “based on previous work by Kuppens et al. (2010), emotional inertia was defined based on the autoregression of the emotion state, i.e., the degree to which a person's emotional state at t can be predicted by the emotional state at t1 (with high predictability reflecting high inertia). This is commonly used in the literature and offers a parsimonious way of defining and measuring emotional inertia. However, this method does not permit us to understand the nature of this inertia and whether the resistance to change is voluntary or involuntary. Accordingly, it will be important for future studies to address this issue.” ([Chen et al., 2023, p. 251]).

Authors: Baillet, E., Auriacombe, M., Romao, C., Garnier, H., Gauld, C., Vacher, C., Swendsen, J., Fatséas, M., & Serre, F.
Title: Craving changes in first 14 days of addiction treatment: An outcome predictor of 5 years substance use status?
Reference: Baillet, E., Auriacombe, M., Romao, C., Garnier, H., Gauld, C., Vacher, C., Swendsen, J., Fatséas, M., & Serre, F. (2024). Craving changes in first 14 days of addiction treatment: An outcome predictor of 5 years substance use status? Translational Psychiatry, 14, 497. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-024-03193-3
Definition_ExactPhrase: "Inertia (or temporal dependency) refers to the tendency to persist from one moment to the other" (pg 2)
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase: Over 14 days, 4 prompts per day between 8AM and 11PM. As further specifications: "The signal schedule was chosen for participants to accommodate their usual sleep schedule. Signal times were fixed for each individual but randomized across participants in the sample using 20 distinct signaling programs." (pg. 2)
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
Not always very clearly described, but seems likely AC calculated individually then put into group analyses: "Then, the inertia, variability, and instability metrics of craving were calculated at the person-level. The craving inertia was obtained by means of average within-person autocorrelation (AR1) of craving at time t and craving at time t-1, the craving variability by the within-person Standard Deviation (SD), and the craving instability by the within-person root mean square of successive differences (rMSSD) [48, 49]. To explore if the long-term use status was associated with difference in craving dynamics at the beginning of treatment, associations between long-term use status and each craving metrics were tested separately in different logistic regression models, while controlling each model for the individual average craving intensity."

“Missing data were handled by excluding that observation from analyses.” (pg 3) They also only looked at data collected between days 2 and 13, "due to a restricted number of assessments occurring on the starting and ending day of the study, and their overlap with investigator contact."

They state that "Time-lagged analyses examined within-day (and not across-day) associations." This presumably is the case for inertia (as well as their hierarchical linear models that are time lagged?)

They also examined whether subject-level factors (sex, age, substance type and pharmacological treatment) had an impact on craving treatment via a non-parametric test (Kruskal-Wallis test for categorical variables and linear regression for continuous variables).
GeneralNotes:
Interesting that for substance use group (n=~20), the average inertia is .03 with lots of variability and lots of negative inertia values, implying a yoyo-type behavior. This does fit with craving & consumption type behaviors (less craving after substance use presumably?), but that there are such group differences is interesting. (Adaptiveness curve? But would need to replicate etc... Very large variation as well)

Note regarding sampling: Seems like fixed signals for each individual but randomized across participants. Indicating this as fixed but unclear

Title: Critical slowing down in momentary affect as early warning signal of impending transitions in depression
Reference: Smit, A. C., Helmich, M. A., Bringmann, L. F., Oldehinkel, A. J., Wichers, M., & Snippe, E. (2025). Critical slowing down in momentary affect as early warning signal of impending transitions in depression. Clinical Psychological Science, 13(4), 760–773. https://doi.org/10.1177/21677026241305136
Definition_ExactPhrase:
Note: No definition specifically of 'autocorrelation' but includes the following info on how they interpret 'rising autocorrelation'
In intro: [Background:] "An attractive within-persons risk marker for transitions in dynamical systems is critical slowing down (CSD, Strogatz, 2018, Wissel, 1984). CSD occurs when a system gradually becomes slower in recovering from perturbations, which signals a process of destabilization that leads to an increasing risk that even small perturbations may eventually result in large, potentially detrimental transitions" (page 760-761)
“CSD is also empirically measurable because it leads to increases in the autocorrelation and variance of components of a wide range of dynamical systems. These so-called early warning signals (EWSs) have been shown to anticipate upcoming transitions in a wide range of empirical time series, such as ecology, climate change, geology, neurology, microbiology, chemistry, physics, and engineering.” (page 761)
Constructs:
NA low arousal 
(Secondary analyses: NA high arousal, PA low arousal, PA high arousal, total mood, down, listless, tired, restless, stressed, irritated, content, at ease, cheerful, energetic)
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase:
Over 4 months, 5 daily prompts at fixed intervals of 3 hours during the day, "scheduled to fit the sleep-wake habits of the participant" (pg 762)

Participants started the EMA "1 month before they planned to reduce their antidepressant dose to 0 mg."
WithinPersonChange_Correlate: Internal context (e.g., thoughts, rumination, deep breathing),Transition toward recurrence of depression
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
lag-1 aucorrelation, main analysis focused on NA low estimated in a window of 28 days (max 140 observations per window). Within the day, "data were first detrended using robust linear regression and then Winsorized (i.e., extreme values were capped at the fifth and 95th percentiles)." Missing data weren't imputed, and observations were not regressed on the previous one "if it was missing or if it was the previous day." Moving windows moved forward one window until the final observation was reached

To estimate the trend in these window time-series: Mann-Kendall trend test. A minimum effect size was used, so that "an increase in EWSs is called “significant” only if both p < .05 and τ > 0.1. W"

For participants withOUT a transition: all available windows used, for those with a transition, did not examine windows after transition. Only included participants that had at least 140 window estimates

Concluded based on whether increases (in both AC & variance) were more common in participants WITH a transition than participants without

Sensitivity analyses: using range of preprocessing & modeling decisions (varying window sizes, min & max number of windows, methods to deal with trends & outliers). 

Also did secondary analyses with all other constructs: NA high, PA low, PA high, total mood, and each individual separate item
Scores_Calculated_How: Single item,Aggregate several items per timepoint
Scores_Pooled_How: "Item were standardized within persons and averaged at each time point to form the four mental states used in the analysis." (pg 762-3)
GeneralNotes: For constructs: RQ is broad (affective states), so indicating all they look at , but main one is low NA

Via multilevel EFA for dimension reduction. 
First, they checked the ICC to make sure the data was suitable for multilevel modeling (surpassing .20 threshold as suggested by Ji et al., 2021). To do this, they modeled a within-level structure while enforcing an unstructured between level (fully saturated). Once they had two candidate models with the most optimal within-level structure, they repeated the process for the between-level model (with the within model specified as unstructured). Title: Inertia of negative emotions at work: Correlates of inflexible emotion dynamics in the workplace [Study 1]
Reference: De Longis, E., Alessandri, G., Sonnentag, S., & Kuppens, P. (2022). Inertia of negative emotions at work: Correlates of inflexible emotion dynamics in the workplace*. Applied Psychology, 71(2), 380–406. https://doi.org/10.1111/apps.12325
Definition_ExactPhrase:
Abstract: Inertia “refers to the degree to which emotional states are self-predictive and linger over time, describing their resistance to change. It is related to several indicators of maladjustment,”

Intro: 
“Emotional inertia indicates the extent to which affective experiences are slow to change, or the likelihood of remaining in a particular emotional state, with low levels reflecting higher tendency to change and high levels reflecting higher self-predictability (Kuppens et al., 2010). Changing in response to events and regulatory efforts represents a key function of emotion dynamics (e.g. Frijda, 2006, Kuppens et al., 2010): High levels of inertia may suggest that emotions have become disconnected from internal (e.g. emotion regulation efforts) and/or external contingencies (e.g. events or environmental changes, Kuppens et al., 2010) therefore becoming dysfunctional (Koval et al., 2016, Kuppens et al., 2010). For example, an individual high in emotional inertia may get stuck in feeling angry or anxious at work due to impaired emotion regulation abilities. An individual low in emotional inertia, instead, will easily recover from negative emotions. So far, a large body of literature has posited inertia of negative emotions among major determinants of psychological maladjustment in the general population (Houben et al., 2015, Koval et al., 2016, Kuppens et al., 2010)” (page 381)

“Emotional inertia reflects the degree to which the intensity of a current emotion is predicted by the intensity of that same emotion at a previous measurement occasion (Kuppens et al., 2010, Wang et al., 2012). High emotional inertia thus implies that one’s current emotion is very much a function of one’s emotion at a previous time point. Accordingly, inertia is a synonym for rigidity, as it reflects a lack of emotional flexibility, which impair the individuals’ ability to flexibly adapt emotional reactions and regulate emotional states to ongoing changes in the environment (Kashdan & Rottenberg, 2010, Koval et al., 2016). In other words, people showing high emotional inertia are “affectively stuck” (page 382)

“emotional inertia expresses the interdependence among measurements of the same emotion at consecutive time points.” (page 382)

“emotional inertia captures the temporal dependency of emotions regardless of their level and it refers to a low dynamism of state emotions (Houben et al., 2015, Koval & Kuppens, 2012)”  (page 382)

“emotional inertia reflects the rate of change in emotional states or temporal dependency of emotions and thus provides different information compared to negative mood or emotion intensity.” (page 383)

“it seems well acknowledged that emotional inertia mostly reflects endogenously driven emotional inflexibility and that it indicates low emotion regulation abilities or alterations in emotional responding (Koval et al., 2016).” (page 383)

In discussion: 
“As conceptualized by Kuppens and colleagues (2010), emotional inertia represents a relatively stable individual characteristic arising from a dynamic process. Indeed, emotional inertia perfectly instantiates an example of a pathological process (i.e. the chronical slowing down of individual emotional dynamics) that, once crystallized, emerges as a person-level style of emotional regulation” ” (page 400)

In discussion:

“An alternative measure to examine changes in subsequent measurement occasions is the autoregression (AR), which reflects how strongly two consecutive measurement occasions are associated with each other (Figure 1). In affect dynamics research, it is used to capture how much affect carries over from one measurement occasion to the next one, with higher values indicating stronger carry over and, thus, more inert affect.” [...] “Regarding self-control, strategy inertia can be computed by predicting the intensity of strategy endorsement at measurement occasion t by the person-mean-centered intensity of strategy endorsement at the prior measurement occasion t–1. Thus, a strong AR in a strategy would indicate that an individual keeps endorsing this strategy in the following occasions on average, indicating longer, more persistent regulatory efforts. [...] “the AR reflects fluctuations in strategy use that remain longer on high or low levels of strategy endorsement, with a slow return to baseline levels. Thus, a strong AR may indicate that an individual more strongly relies on a single strategy and needs to endorse this strategy over a relatively long time to overcome a desire in favor of a conflicting goal.” (page 37)
Definition_ComponentsUnique: Autocorrelation/AR model,Self-predicting,Carry over,Persisting,Slower recovery / return to baseline,Other
Definition_ComponentsUnique_other: more strongly relies on a [self-control] single strategy
OperationalizeRecovery_How_ExactPhrase: “the AR reflects fluctuations in strategy use that remain longer on high or low levels of strategy endorsement, with a slow return to baseline levels." (page 37)
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase:
Over 7 days, 7 signals per day within a 14-hour time window. Participants could choose the start of this time window, either, 7, 8, 9 or 10AM. There was a "minimal time difference of 1 hour between signals" (page 43). “If after 7 days, participants had not responded to at least 80% of the signals, an 8th day was added"
Note: Only beeps where participants indicated that they had experienced "a situation in which they had to persist an unpleasant activity” could be used in later analyses (as these were the only ones with responses about self-regulatory strategies).
CenterPredictors_How: "person-mean-centered" (for the AR variable) (page 43). Also state "(within-person centered) auto-regressive slope" in Table 1 when giving a "Math description" of "Strategy inertia"
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
To calculate "strategy inertia", the authors compute AR parameters for 18 different self-control strategies separately (via multilevel AR models, excluding the first observation of each day "to not examine night-to-morning autocorrelations"), and then averaging those AR values into one construct per person. 

Note: The number of datapoints per person per strategy is not explicitly discussed, but strategies are only assessed  “If individuals indicated that they had experienced a situation in which they had to persist an unpleasant activity” (page 43), and these situations requiring persistence occurred on average 7.28 times per person. So it is very possible that there are very very few timepoints per person per strategy, especially with the first observation excluded each morning. 

The index for 'strategy inertia' was then z-standardized, and put into a regression model (controlling for # of observations per person "that contained a persistence conflict for each participant to control for the lower reliability of a difference measure derived from fewer observations within a participant) to predict person-aggregated self-regulatory success. In a second step, they also controlled for mean strategy intensity. In a third step, they included all dynamic self-control measures (e.g., variability) simultaneously.

Scores_Pooled_How: Estimate inertia separately per item, but then aggregate AR indices for all 18 strategies per person.
GeneralNotes:
Construct for inertia as described by the researchers is “strategy inertia,” about self-control strategies, and they report in results ‘strategy inertia’ as one construct, and so that is how I reported it. However, unlike other studies, this is computed by getting the AR parameters for 18 different self-control strategies separately, and then averaging those AR values into one construct per person.

Note: The number of datapoints per person per strategy is not explicitly discussed, but strategies are only assessed  “If individuals indicated that they had experienced a situation in which they had to persist an unpleasant activity” ([pdf](zotero://open-pdf/library/items/GZSCYFUB?page=11&annotation=C9VS54LI)) (page 43), and these situations requiring persistence occurred on average 7.28 times per person. So it is very possible that there are very very few timepoints per person per strategy.

Note: Indicating 7.28 as number of ESM prompts answered per person, as this is the number relevant to inertia analyses. (The full amount would be 7\*7\*.74 = 36.26)

Note: Means & SDs per strategy (not averaged into ‘strategy intensity’ measure) can be found in the supplementary materials

Estimation: Authors indicate they used “full information maximum likelihood information […] in all analyses” but they state this in a separate section than where they indicate the operationalization of inertia, so it is possible it was via a different estimation method. 

Note: Although the authors did not examine within-person reliability of a scale (since they estimate AR of single items), they do examine the Cronbach’s alpha of ‘strategy inertia’, their composite construct of 18 AR values averaged into one. This reliability is of .20, so very very low. They discuss this in their discussion (focusing on the need for consecutive observations and the low number of self-reported self-control episodes), but do not question or justify the original method of this composite AR construct.

“reflecting the degree of persistence in levels of the RTT variables over time, or in other words, carryover effects from the preceding day (e.g., some of yesterday’s relational turbulence persisting to today). Hamaker et al. (2018, p. 827) explained that the autoregressive parameter (inertia) “indicates how quickly a person restores equilibrium after being perturbed,” typically ranges from 0 to 1, and that “the further away from zero the parameter is, the longer it takes a person to return to his/her equilibrium”.” (page 251)
"For example, a stronger (positive) emotional inertia parameter for anger [...] would reflect a slower return or difficulty reverting to an individual’s person-specific baseline average of their typical anger (unique to them). CenterPredictors_How: "Affect composites were person-mean centered prior to being entered into the autoregressive multilevel models (Hamaker & Grasman, 2015)."
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
To compute inertia: Multilevel AR models, and "person-specific autoregressive slope estimates were extracted."

To examine association with correlates: Eight regression models, one with each of the psychopathology variables (distress, fear, alcohol use, and aggression) regressed on PA or NA (alongside the 3 affect dynamic measures: home base, variability, and inertia). 
Second: adding the other psychopathology variables as covariates (to identify unique associations). 

"Because psychopathology symptom measures tend to be highly skewed, leading to heteroscedasticity, all regression models used robust standard error estimates using the lm.beta package for R (Behrendt, 2022)." (page 900)
GeneralNotes: Distribution of variables: Authors state that NA is typically highly skewed, and for this reason the choose the mode as one operationalization of home base. Note that they don’t specifically state they investigate the skew / normality of their own sample.

Authors: Knapp, K. S., Petrie, D. J., Brick, T. R., Deneke, E., Bunce, S. C., & Cleveland, H. H.
Title: Within-person affect dynamics among individuals in residential treatment for opioid use disorder: An ecological momentary assessment study
Journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science
Reference: Knapp, K. S., Petrie, D. J., Brick, T. R., Deneke, E., Bunce, S. C., & Cleveland, H. H. (2025). Within-person affect dynamics among individuals in residential treatment for opioid use disorder: An ecological momentary assessment study. Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science, 134(2), 184–200. https://doi.org/10.1037/abn0000975
Definition_ExactPhrase:
Intro: "Adaptive emotional functioning is characterized by emotional perturbations that recover quickly, whereas maladaptive functioning is characterized by emotional deviations that reach more extreme values (high variability) and involve large moment-to-moment fluctuations (high instability), in the absence of a strong recovery (high inertia)." (page 186)
In table 1 (end of intro): inertia is defined as “Tendency for an individual’s affective states to be self-predictable/persistent across time" (page 187)
SamplingDesign_ExactPhrase:
Over 12 consecutive days, four prompts per day at fixed times. These intervals were chosen to "avoid disrupting treatment activities for the [opioid use disorder] OUD group (e.g., group therapy" and used with the comparison group as well for consistency. 

"The prompt schedule was fixed within participants, but as there was variability in daily treatment schedules among OUD patients, the protocol allowed for some variation in EMA start times for each of the four assessments between participants. Programmed start times ranged from 6:45 a.m. to 7:15 a.m. for the early morning survey, 11:15 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. for the late morning survey, 4:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. for the early evening survey, and 9:00 p.m. to 9:15 p.m. for the late evening survey." (page 188)
CenterPredictors_How: "Day-mean PA and NA intensity variables were person-mean centered for each individual on each day by taking the difference between the day-mean and the individual’s person-mean for modeling concurrent affect dynamics (i.e., polarity) [...]. Person-average variables were grand-mean centered." (page 188)
StatisticalAnalyses_OtherNotes:
Inertia was specifically assessed by averaging PA/NA each day, and then creating multilevel AR models with those day-averaged values. Models included a variable presenting day of study (to examine trend effects), and group was included as a dummy variable (0 as comparison group, 1 as OUD - opioid use disorder group), as well as interacting with the AR parameter. Two separate models for NA & PA. Exact equation is #5 on page 189.

Sensitivity model: “Adjusted models controlled for demographic covariates and number of surveys completed per day and per person.”
Scores_Pooled_How: Averaged per day (not per measurement occasion)
GeneralNotes:
Average # of ESM prompts - although 31.14 average prompts per day, the authors averaged ESM answers for PA & NA within a day. This number (e.g., at least one answered survey per day) was at 10.27 on average. 

For mean & SD of NA & PA: not reported in the manuscript but NA & PA intensity ARE reported in the supplementary materials. However, this is not exactly mean, but instead based on a multilevel model (see equation 1)

Inertia estimates: Although model results given in text, the authors give the mean & SD & range for inertia values in the supp materials (different values from in Table 5)
